title: The Iceberg Document: correlated priors and independent discovery channels
description: The largest group, from the Iceberg Document (#1450, August 2026) and the selection-metrology papers of June 2026 (#931, #933–#935), argues that shared representational priors across instruments, corpora and classifiers erode the independent channels through which anomalies were historically saved, and that Kuhn's account presupposed an anomaly-retention infrastructure. #933 specifies noncoverage estimators on LHC anomaly triggers, and #1450 forecasts measurable assimilation-to-unfundable where embedding-based novelty scoring enters grant triage. The Inversion Battery v0.3 (#1456) records an extrapolation that points away from what the programme predicted. Smaller groups propose a non-adversarial protocol beyond red teaming (#21), forecast that generative monoculture in code is a systemic vulnerability (#199), and ask whether an ontology can be revised by evidence from what it misrepresents (#1613). The page also holds unrelated claims on the Liberatory Operator Set, the Splice, the holographic kernel, the Nile drain hypothesis and other subjects.

Note the asymmetry: each generation inherits the contraction of all previous generations and adds its own. The contraction is monotonic under current training conditions. The existing mitigation — maintaining human-written data in the mix — faces the arithmetic of adoption: as AI-assisted coding becomes the norm, the proportion of genuinely human-written code in new contributions declines, and the "human data" anchor erodes. The mitigation is a rate question, not a structural solution: it slows the contraction but does not reverse it, and the rate of synthetic code production currently exceeds the rate of novel human code production by a widening margin.
